blocks.p: Now I saw in my dream that they had not gone far before the river and the road parted for a while. They were very sorry for this, yet they did not dare leave the road. Now the road away from the river was rough, and their feet were tender from all their travels, so the spirits of the pilgrims grew very discouraged because of the way. [Num. 21:4] And as they went on, they kept wishing for a better road.
A little ahead of them, on the left side of the road, there was a meadow, with a stile for climbing over the fence into it; and that meadow is called By-path Meadow.

“If this meadow runs alongside our road,” said Christian to his companion, “let’s go over into it.” He went to the stile to look, and sure enough, a path ran along beside the road on the other side of the fence. “It’s just what I wanted,” said Christian. “This is the easiest going. Come on, good Hopeful, let’s go over.”
“But what if this path leads us out of the way?”
“That’s not likely,” said Christian. “Look, doesn’t it run right alongside the road?”

So Hopeful, persuaded by his companion, followed him over the stile. Once they were over and on the path, they found it very easy on their feet. And looking ahead, they saw a man walking the same way they were, whose name was Vain-confidence. They called after him and asked where the path led.
“To the Celestial Gate,” he said.
“Look,” said Christian, “didn’t I tell you? This proves we’re right.”
So they followed, and he went on ahead of them. But then night came on, and it grew very dark, so that the two behind lost sight of the one in front.

Then the one in front, Vain-confidence by name, not seeing the way before him, fell into a deep pit [Isa. 9:16] that the prince of those grounds had dug on purpose to catch vainglorious fools, and he was dashed to pieces in the fall.
Christian and his companion heard him fall. They called out to find out what had happened, but no one answered; they heard only a groaning.
“Where are we now?” said Hopeful.
Christian was silent, suspecting that he had led him out of the way. And now it began to rain, and to thunder and lightning in a very terrifying way, and the water rose fast.
Then Hopeful groaned to himself, “Oh, if only I had kept to the road!”
“Who could have thought this path would lead us out of the way?” said Christian.
“I was afraid of it from the very first, and that’s why I gave you that gentle warning. I would have spoken more plainly, except that you are older than I am.”
“Good brother, don’t be offended. I’m sorry I’ve brought you out of the way and put you into such terrible danger. Please, my brother, forgive me. I didn’t do it with any bad intent.”
“Be comforted, my brother, for I forgive you. And believe this too: it will turn out for our good.”
“I’m glad to have such a merciful brother with me. But we mustn’t stand here like this. Let’s try to go back.”
“But, good brother, let me go first.”
“No, please, let me go first, so that if there is any danger I’ll be the first to meet it, since it’s my fault we have both gone out of the way.”
“No,” said Hopeful, “you shall not go first. Your mind is troubled, and it may lead you out of the way again.”

Then, to encourage them, they heard a voice saying, “Set your heart on the highway, the road that you took. Turn back.” [Jer. 31:21] But by this time the waters had risen very high, which made the way back very dangerous. (Then I thought: it is easier to go out of the way when we are in it than to get back in when we are out.) Still, they ventured to go back; but it was so dark, and the flood so high, that on the way they nearly drowned nine or ten times.
Nor could they, with all the skill they had, get back to the stile that night. So at last, finding a little shelter, they sat down there to wait for daybreak; but being weary, they fell asleep.

Now not far from where they lay there was a castle called Doubting Castle, and its owner was Giant Despair; and it was on his grounds that they were sleeping. Getting up early in the morning and walking up and down his fields, he caught Christian and Hopeful asleep on his land. In a grim and surly voice he told them to wake up, and asked where they were from and what they were doing on his grounds. They told him they were pilgrims and had lost their way.
“You have trespassed against me tonight,” said the Giant, “by trampling over my land and lying on it, and so you must come along with me.”

They were forced to go, because he was stronger than they were. And they had little to say, for they knew they were in the wrong. So the Giant drove them ahead of him and put them into his castle, into a very dark dungeon, foul and stinking to the spirits of these two men. [Ps. 88:18] Here they lay from Wednesday morning until Saturday night, without one bite of bread or drop of drink, without light, without anyone to ask how they were. They were in a terrible state, and far from friends and anyone they knew. And in this place Christian had double sorrow, because it was by his ill-advised counsel that they had been brought into this misery.

v: The pilgrims now, to gratify the flesh,
go seeking ease; but oh, how they afresh
plunge headlong into griefs they never knew!
Who seeks to please the flesh, undoes himself too.

blocks.p: Now Giant Despair had a wife, and her name was Misgiving. When he had gone to bed, he told his wife what he had done: that he had taken a couple of prisoners and thrown them into his dungeon for trespassing on his grounds. Then he asked her what he had best do with them next. She asked him who they were, where they came from, and where they were going, and he told her. Then she advised him that when he got up in the morning he should beat them without mercy.

So when he got up, he took a vicious club of crab-apple wood and went down into the dungeon to them. First he began to abuse them as if they were dogs, though they had never given him one ill word. Then he fell on them and beat them so fearfully that they could not help themselves, or even turn over on the floor. That done, he withdrew and left them there to grieve over their misery and mourn in their distress. And all that day they did nothing but sigh and lament bitterly.

The next night his wife talked with him about them further, and when she learned they were still alive, she advised him to urge them to do away with themselves. So when morning came, he went to them in the same surly way as before, and seeing how sore they were from the beating he had given them the day before, he told them that since they were never going to get out of that place, their only course was to make an end of themselves at once, with knife, rope, or poison. “For why,” he said, “should you choose life, when it comes with so much bitterness?”

But they begged him to let them go. At that he gave them an ugly look and rushed at them, and he would certainly have finished them himself, except that he fell into one of his fits (for sometimes, in sunny weather, he had fits) and lost the use of his hand for a time. So he withdrew and left them as before, to consider what to do. Then the prisoners discussed between themselves whether it was best to take his advice or not, and this is how they talked.

“Brother,” said Christian, “what shall we do? The life we’re living now is miserable. For my part, I don’t know whether it’s better to live like this or to die at once. ‘My soul would choose strangling rather than life,’ and the grave would be easier for me than this dungeon. [Job 7:15] Shall we be ruled by the Giant?”

“It’s true, our present condition is dreadful,” said Hopeful, “and death would be far more welcome to me than staying like this forever. But still, let’s think. The Lord of the country we are going to has said, ‘You shall not murder’—not even another man. How much more, then, are we forbidden to take the Giant’s advice and kill ourselves! Besides, a man who kills another can only murder his body; but one who kills himself kills body and soul at once. And more than that, my brother, you talk of ease in the grave; but have you forgotten the hell where murderers certainly go? ‘For no murderer has eternal life.’

“And let’s consider again that the law is not all in the hands of Giant Despair. Others, as far as I understand, have been taken by him just as we have, and yet have escaped from his hand. Who knows whether the God who made the world may cause Giant Despair to die? Or whether some time or other he may forget to lock us in? Or whether before long he may have another of his fits in front of us and lose the use of his limbs? If that ever happens again, I for one am determined to take heart like a man and try my utmost to get out from under his hand. I was a fool not to try it before. But in any case, my brother, let’s be patient and endure a while. The time may come that brings us a happy release. But let’s not be our own murderers.”
With these words Hopeful steadied his brother’s mind for the present; so they stayed together in the dark that day, in their sad and wretched condition.

Toward evening the Giant went down into the dungeon again to see whether his prisoners had taken his advice. But when he got there he found them alive; and truly, alive was all they were. What with the lack of bread and water, and the wounds they had received when he beat them, they could do little more than breathe. But, I say, he found them alive, and at this he fell into a terrible rage and told them that since they had disobeyed his advice, it would go worse with them than if they had never been born.

At this they trembled greatly, and I think Christian fainted. But when he came to himself a little, they took up their discussion again about the Giant’s advice, and whether they had better take it after all. Once more Christian seemed to be in favor of it; but Hopeful made his second reply, as follows.

“My brother,” he said, “don’t you remember how brave you have been before now? Apollyon could not crush you, nor could all you heard and saw and felt in the Valley of the Shadow of Death. What hardship, terror, and bewilderment you have already been through! And are you now nothing but fear? You see that I am in the dungeon with you, a far weaker man by nature than you are. This Giant has wounded me as well as you, and has cut off the bread and water from my mouth too, and I mourn with you here without the light. But let’s be a little more patient. Remember how you played the man at Vanity Fair, and were not afraid of the chain, or the cage, or even of a bloody death. So let’s bear up with patience as well as we can, if only to avoid the shame of being found in a state that does not become a Christian.”
Now when night had come again, and the Giant and his wife were in bed, she asked him about the prisoners, and whether they had taken his advice.
“They are sturdy rogues,” he replied. “They would rather bear every hardship than do away with themselves.”

“Take them into the castle yard tomorrow,” she said, “and show them the bones and skulls of the ones you have already finished off, and make them believe that before the week is out you will tear them to pieces too, as you did the others before them.”
So when morning came, the Giant went to them again, and took them into the castle yard, and showed them, as his wife had told him.

“These,” he said, “were pilgrims once, as you are, and they trespassed on my grounds, as you have done; and when I saw fit, I tore them to pieces. And so, within ten days, I will do to you. Go on, get down to your den again.” And with that he beat them all the way back.

So all day Saturday they lay there in a pitiful state, as before. When night came, and Mrs. Misgiving and her husband the Giant had gone to bed, they took up the subject of their prisoners again, and the old Giant wondered why he could not bring them to their end either by his blows or by his advice.
“I’m afraid,” his wife replied, “that they are living in hope that someone will come to rescue them, or that they have lock picks on them, and hope to escape that way.”
“Do you think so, my dear?” said the Giant. “Then I’ll search them in the morning.”
Well, on Saturday, about midnight, they began to pray, and they went on praying until almost daybreak.

A little before it was light, good Christian, like a man half dazed, broke out in an impassioned speech. “What a fool I am,” he said, “to lie like this in a stinking dungeon, when I could just as well be walking free! I have a key here in my coat called Promise that will, I am convinced, open any lock in Doubting Castle.”
“That’s good news,” said Hopeful. “Good brother, take it out and try it.”

Then Christian took it out and began to try it on the dungeon door; and as he turned the key, the bolt slid back, and the door flew open with ease, and Christian and Hopeful both came out. Then he went to the outer door that leads into the castle yard, and with his key he opened that door too. After that he went to the iron gate, for that had to be opened as well; and that lock was terribly hard to turn, yet the key did open it. Then they pushed the gate open to make their escape as fast as they could. But as it opened, the gate creaked so loudly that it woke Giant Despair, who jumped up to chase his prisoners and felt his limbs give way, for his fits had seized him again, so that he could not go after them at all. Then they went on and came to the King’s highway again, and so were safe, because they were outside his jurisdiction.

Now when they had climbed back over the stile, they began to work out between them what they could do at that stile to keep those who came after them from falling into the hands of Giant Despair. They agreed to set up a pillar there, and to carve on its side this sentence: Over this stile is the way to Doubting Castle, which is kept by Giant Despair, who despises the King of the Celestial Country and seeks to destroy his holy pilgrims. And so many who came after read what was written and escaped the danger. This done, they sang:

v: Out of the way we went, and then we found
what it is like to tread forbidden ground.
And let all those who follow us take care,
lest carelessness should make them fare as we fare,
lest for their trespass they be prisoners there,
whose castle’s Doubting, and whose name’s Despair.
